endorsements.quote: AI methods can be used to detect algorithmic bias (e.g [ 59 ]), however rigorous testing of generalization to minority populations, and improving the diversity of the underlying datasets used to train models are critical to longer term efforts.

Interpretability can help with this, but specific procedures can be used to quantify drift (i.e., differences between training and test data sets) [ 60 ] so that models can be retrained or recalibrated once deployed.
Interpretability varies according to the types of machine learning used in a solution, and solutions can be made ‘interpretable by design’ [ 42 , 51 ].
Designing and implementing models that are compatible with existing clinical workflows is key for advancing dementia therapeutics.

AI methods can be used to detect algorithmic bias (e.g [ 59 ]), however rigorous testing of generalization to minority populations, and improving the diversity of the underlying datasets used to train models are critical to longer term efforts.

unlisted_practices: Prospectively validate AI stratification tools in clinical trials by locking the subgroup definition before trial initiation.
Ensure AI-guided patient selection at different stages of the trial recruitment funnel does not systematically exclude patients with particular demographics.
Design AI models to be robust to missing or degraded real-world data, for example through probabilistic imputation.
Use pre-planned subgroup sampling, stratified randomisation, and pre-specified subgroup statistical analysis plans in trials when it is uncertain which subgroups benefit.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/commentary paper discussing the use of multimodal AI for patient stratification in dementia clinical trials and real-world care.
